paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend. The Teacher had the wisdom, the money, the gardens, the singers, all of it, and he still said everything was "futile, a pursuit of the wind" (Ecclesiastes 2:11). He was no beginner. He ran the experiment on himself, with his mind still guiding him, and he did it until he could see what was worthwhile in the few days of a life (Ecclesiastes 2:3). If a king with no limits comes back with "nothing to be gained under the sun," that tells you something about where we keep looking.

So what do we do with that? I think the passage is gently taking a thing out of your hands. Maybe you've got a goal in mind, like the bigger paycheck, the cleaner house, the full calendar, the finished project. I chase the PERFECT batch every week, and the oven keeps teaching me the same lesson. The Teacher isn't saying you should stop working or stop enjoying good things. He's saying that none of it can carry the weight of being your whole reason.

Here's why that matters to you today. When you wake up tired and wonder why all the effort feels like holding wind, you're not broken, friend. The Teacher felt it too, and he wrote it down for us. The searching is real, and it points beyond what the sun can show us, and that's exactly where the rest of this book keeps leading. The story isn't over, so keep your oven warm and keep listening.
